front_blocks.md: Which type of wave, transverse or longitudinal, can travel through a vacuum, and why?

back_blocks.md: **Transverse** waves can travel through a vacuum because they do not need particles to propagate. **Longitudinal** waves need particles to propagate, so they cannot travel through a vacuum.

front_blocks.md: Longitudinal waves, such as sound, can be polarised.

back_blocks.md: Only **transverse** waves can be polarised, because polarisation restricts oscillation to one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel. Longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to the direction of travel, so they cannot be polarised.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

Longitudinal waves, such as sound, can be polarised.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

Only **transverse** waves can be polarised, because polarisation restricts oscillation to one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel. Longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to the direction of travel, so they cannot be polarised.

front_blocks.md: A displacement–time graph shows a wave oscillating periodically. Can this graph alone tell you whether the wave is transverse or longitudinal?

back_blocks.md: No. Both wave types can produce the same displacement–time graph shape. To identify the wave type you need to know whether the particle displacement is **perpendicular** (transverse) or **parallel** (longitudinal) to the direction of energy transfer.
